clinicalPearls: A rare, aggressive mature lymphoid leukaemia in which prolymphocytes dominate the blood
Occurs in B-cell and T-cell forms, with the T-cell type being the more common and particularly aggressive
Typically presents in older adults with a very high lymphocyte count, marked splenomegaly and often minimal lymphadenopathy
T-cell disease may involve the skin, serous effusions and central nervous system
Prolymphocytes are larger than mature lymphocytes and have a prominent central nucleolus
T-cell prolymphocytic leukaemia commonly shows abnormalities involving the TCL1 locus and chromosome 11 (ATM)
It is distinguished from chronic lymphocytic leukaemia by morphology, immunophenotype and its aggressive course
reference.pathophysiology: Prolymphocytic leukaemia is a clonal proliferation of intermediate-sized lymphoid cells arrested at the prolymphocyte stage. In the T-cell form, rearrangements activating the TCL1 oncogene, together with ATM inactivation from chromosome 11 abnormalities, drive proliferation and impair DNA damage responses, producing an aggressive disease with high tumour burden. The B-cell form is a distinct clonal B-cell disorder. Extensive marrow, splenic and blood involvement accounts for the very high counts, cytopenias and organomegaly, while tissue tropism in T-cell disease explains skin and serosal involvement.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia with increased prolymphocytes
Mantle cell lymphoma in leukaemic phase
additionalInvestigations: Flow cytometry to define B- or T-cell lineage and immunophenotype
Cytogenetics and molecular testing (including TCL1 and ATM/chromosome 11 assessment)
Imaging to assess splenomegaly and any nodal or extranodal disease
redFlags: Very high and rapidly rising lymphocyte count with cytopenias
Central nervous system or serosal involvement in T-cell disease
reference.prognosis: T-cell prolymphocytic leukaemia is aggressive with historically poor survival, although targeted antibody therapy and, where feasible, allogeneic transplantation have improved outcomes; the B-cell form is also aggressive but somewhat variable.
pitfalls: Misclassifying it as chronic lymphocytic leukaemia and underestimating its aggressiveness
Failing to distinguish B-cell from T-cell disease, which affects treatment
Overlooking central nervous system or skin involvement
Delaying treatment in a rapidly progressive leukaemia
management: Treat T-cell prolymphocytic leukaemia primarily with the anti-CD52 monoclonal antibody alemtuzumab, to which it is uniquely responsive
Consolidate responders with allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation where fitness and a donor allow, as the only potentially durable option
Treat the B-cell form with chemoimmunotherapy and targeted agents such as rituximab-based regimens, and BTK inhibitors or venetoclax where molecular features indicate

Provide supportive care with transfusion for cytopenias, tumour lysis prophylaxis, and antimicrobial prophylaxis against viral, fungal and Pneumocystis infection with CMV monitoring during alemtuzumab
Address extranodal T-cell disease including skin infiltration, serous effusions and central nervous system involvement
Enrol in clinical trials given the aggressive course, and involve palliative care for patients unfit for intensive therapy
